Rooney started the season with a goal in the first league game at [The Hawthorns](/wiki/The_Hawthorns "The Hawthorns") against West Bromwich Albion. Rooney played a one-two with [Ashley Young](/wiki/Ashley_Young "Ashley Young") before a sharp turn and finish from outside the box which found the bottom corner of the goal. He also scored in the second game of the season, at home to Tottenham Hotspur, when he headed in a Ryan Giggs cross.[[165]](#cite_note-165) In late August, Rooney scored his 150th goal for United, the first of a [hat-trick](/wiki/Hat-trick "Hat-trick"), helping to beat Arsenal 8–2. Rooney won man of the match, scoring two free kicks, a penalty, and also contributing an assist for [Nani](/wiki/Nani_(footballer) "Nani (footballer)"). On 10 September, Rooney scored another hat-trick in a 5–0 away win over Bolton Wanderers on 10 September, becoming only the fourth player in Premier League history to score a hat-trick in consecutive games.[[166]](#cite_note-166) These goals brought him level with [Bobby Charlton](/wiki/Bobby_Charlton "Bobby Charlton") on seven United hat-tricks, joint fourth on the all-time list behind [Denis Law](/wiki/Denis_Law "Denis Law"), [Jack Rowley](/wiki/Jack_Rowley "Jack Rowley") and [Dennis Viollet](/wiki/Dennis_Viollet "Dennis Viollet").[[167]](#cite_note-167) After the fallout from his red card against [Montenegro](/wiki/Montenegro_national_football_team "Montenegro national football team") on international duty, Rooney was left out of the starting line-up against Liverpool on 15 October 2011.[[168]](#cite_note-168) He returned to action on 18 October 2011, where he scored two goals in the [Champions League group stage](/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_UEFA_Champions_League_group_stage "2011–12 UEFA Champions League group stage") match against [Oțelul Galați](/wiki/FC_O%C8%9Belul_Gala%C8%9Bi "FC Oțelul Galați") and surpassed his former teammate Paul Scholes as the highest-scoring Englishman in Champions League history.[[169]](#cite_note-169)

Christie died on 12 January 1976 at age 85 from [natural causes](/wiki/Natural_causes "Natural causes") at her home at Winterbrook House.[[84]](#cite_note-:0-91)[[85]](#cite_note-92) Upon her death, two [West End](/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") theatres – the [St. Martin's](/wiki/St_Martin%27s_Theatre "St Martin's Theatre"), where *[The Mousetrap](/wiki/The_Mousetrap "The Mousetrap")* was playing, and [the Savoy](/wiki/Savoy_Theatre "Savoy Theatre"), which was home to a revival of *Murder at the Vicarage* – dimmed their outside lights in her honour.[[34]](#cite_note-:16-36): 373 She was buried in the nearby churchyard of St Mary's, Cholsey, in a plot she had chosen with her husband 10 years previously. The simple funeral service was attended by about 20 newspaper and TV reporters, some having travelled from as far away as South America. Thirty wreaths adorned Christie's grave, including one from the cast of her long-running play *The Mousetrap* and one sent "on behalf of the multitude of grateful readers" by the Ulverscroft Large Print Book Publishers.[[86]](#cite_note-93)

History of the Internet :: 2004–present: Web 2.0, global ubiquity, social media :: The mobile revolution :: chunk_0028
Main articles: [History of mobile phones](/wiki/History_of_mobile_phones "History of mobile phones"), [Mobile web](/wiki/Mobile_web "Mobile web"), and [Responsive web design](/wiki/Responsive_web_design "Responsive web design")

The process of change that generally coincided with Web 2.0 was itself greatly accelerated and transformed only a short time later by the increasing growth in mobile devices. This mobile revolution meant that computers in the form of smartphones became something many people used, took with them everywhere, communicated with, used for photographs and videos they instantly shared or to shop or seek information "on the move" – and used socially, as opposed to items on a desk at home or just used for work.

Location-based services, services using location and other sensor information, and [crowdsourcing](/wiki/Crowdsourcing "Crowdsourcing") (frequently but not always location based), became common, with posts tagged by location, or websites and services becoming location aware. Mobile-targeted websites (such as "m.example.com") became common, designed especially for the new devices used. [Netbooks](/wiki/Netbook "Netbook"), [ultrabooks](/wiki/Ultrabook "Ultrabook"), widespread [4G](/wiki/4G "4G") and [Wi-Fi](/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi"), and mobile chips capable or running at nearly the power of desktops from not many years before on far lower power usage, became enablers of this stage of Internet development, and the term "[App](/wiki/App_(computing) "App (computing)")" (short for "Application program" or "Program") became popularized, as did the "[App store](/wiki/App_store "App store")".

This "mobile revolution" has allowed for people to have a nearly unlimited amount of information at all times. With the ability to access the internet from cell phones came a change in the way media was consumed. Media consumption statistics show that over half of media consumption between those aged 18 and 34 were using a smartphone.[[205]](#cite_note-205)

Topographic map of Okinawa Island

Okinawa is the fifth largest island of Japan. The island has an area of 1,206.99 square kilometers (466.02 sq mi). The coastline is 476 kilometers (296 mi) long.[[44]](#cite_note-toukei2014-44) The straight-line distance is about 106.6 kilometers (66.2 mi) from north to south.[[45]](#cite_note-rekishi-okinawajima73chu-45) Okinawa is in the northeastern end of [Okinawa Prefecture](/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture "Okinawa Prefecture"). Since 1972 over 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of land has been added via [reclamation](/wiki/Land_reclamation "Land reclamation") (0.83% of the island's total area).

It is roughly 640 kilometres (400 mi) south of the main island of Kyushu. Okinawa is connected to nearby islands near a land bridge: [Katsuren Peninsula](/wiki/Katsuren_Peninsula "Katsuren Peninsula") is connected via the [Mid-Sea Road](/wiki/Mid-Sea_Road "Mid-Sea Road") to Henza Island, Miyagi Island, Ikei Island, and Hamahiga Island. Similarly, from the [Motobu Peninsula](/wiki/Motobu_Peninsula "Motobu Peninsula") on the northwestern side, all of [Sesoko-jima](/w/index.php?title=Sesoko-jima&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sesoko-jima (page does not exist)") plus [Yagaji Island](/w/index.php?title=Yagaji_Island&action=edit&redlink=1 "Yagaji Island (page does not exist)") and [Kōri-jima](/w/index.php?title=K%C5%8Dri-jima&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kōri-jima (page does not exist)") are connected by bridges. Okinawa Island has several beaches such as Manza Beach, Emerald Beach, Okuma Beach, Zanpa Beach, Moon Beach and Sunset Beach (Chatan-cho). [Mount Omoto](/wiki/Mount_Omoto "Mount Omoto"), at 525.5 m (1,724 ft), is the highest mountain in Okinawa, with [Mount Yonaha](/wiki/Mount_Yonaha "Mount Yonaha") being the second highest.[[46]](#cite_note-nipponika-46)

Stuyvesant High School opened in September 1904 as Manhattan's first specialized high school.[[14]](#cite_note-nyclpc-15): 5 At the time of its opening, it had 155 students and 12 teachers.[[17]](#cite_note-nyt199209-18)

At first, the school provided a core curriculum of "English, Latin, modern languages, history, mathematics, physics, chemistry, [and] music", as well as a physical education program and a more specialized track of "woodworking, metalworking, mechanical drawing, [and] freehand drawing".[[14]](#cite_note-nyclpc-15): 5 But in June 1908, Maxwell announced that the school's core curriculum would be separated for the rest and that a discrete trade school would operate in the Stuyvesant building in the evening.[[14]](#cite_note-nyclpc-15): 5[[18]](#cite_note-19) Thereafter, Stuyvesant became renowned for excellence in math and science. In 1909, eighty percent of the school's alumni went to college; other high schools sent only 25% to 50% of their graduates to college.[[14]](#cite_note-nyclpc-15): 5[[19]](#cite_note-20)

By 1919, officials were restricting admission based on academic achievement.[[20]](#cite_note-cfs_timeline-21) Stuyvesant implemented a double session plan in 1919 to accommodate the rising number of students: some students would attend in the morning and others in the afternoon and early evening. All students studied a full set of courses. These double sessions ran until spring 1957.[[20]](#cite_note-cfs_timeline-21)[[21]](#cite_note-22) The school implemented a system of entrance examinations in 1934.[[22]](#cite_note-blaufarb1-23) The examination program, developed with the assistance of [Columbia University](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), was expanded in 1938 to include the newly founded [Bronx High School of Science](/wiki/Bronx_High_School_of_Science "Bronx High School of Science").[[14]](#cite_note-nyclpc-15): 5[[22]](#cite_note-blaufarb1-23)

The Technikum was conceived in the early 1900s by the German-Jewish fund [Ezra](/w/index.php?title=Ezra_(German-Jewish_fund)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ezra (German-Jewish fund) (page does not exist)") as a school of engineering and sciences. It was to be the only institution of higher learning in the then [Ottoman Palestine](/wiki/History_of_Palestine#Ottoman_period "History of Palestine"), other than the [Bezalel Academy of Art and Design](/wiki/Bezalel_Academy_of_Art_and_Design "Bezalel Academy of Art and Design") in [Jerusalem](/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem") (founded in 1906).[[12]](#cite_note-13) In October 1913, the board of trustees selected [German](/wiki/German_language "German language") as the language of instruction, provoking a major controversy known as the [War of the Languages](/wiki/War_of_the_Languages "War of the Languages"). After opposition from American and Russian Jews to the use of German, the board of trustees reversed itself in February 1914 and selected Hebrew as the language of instruction. The German name Technikum was also replaced by the Hebrew name Technion.[[3]](#cite_note-technikum-4)[[13]](#cite_note-cie-14)

Technion's cornerstone was laid in 1912, and studies began 12 years later in 1924.[[13]](#cite_note-cie-14) In 1923 [Albert Einstein](/wiki/Albert_Einstein "Albert Einstein") visited and planted the now-famous first [palm tree](/wiki/Arecaceae "Arecaceae"), as an initiative of [Nobel](/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") tradition. The first palm tree still stands today in front of the old Technion building, which is now the MadaTech museum, in the Hadar neighborhood.
